title: Buying triggers: the reasons clients act, and how to speak to them honestly
audience: Owners and marketers in any service business who want messages that match what clients are trying to achieve.
learningOutcomes: Name the five common buying triggers and give one service example of each
Rank the triggers for a target group using real enquiries, reviews or messages
Write a client message for each chosen trigger that makes no unverified claim and is checked for health-claim and consumer-law risk

instruction.heading: A trigger is the reason a client acts
instruction.body: A client moves from interest to booking when something they care about becomes urgent or valuable enough to act on. That is the buying trigger. A message works best when it speaks to a trigger the client already feels and shows how the service answers it. A trigger is not the feature list. A carpet clean is a feature. The trigger might be a landlord who needs a bond returned in full, or a family who wants a tidy home before visitors arrive.

instruction.heading: Five triggers to test
instruction.body: Test five common triggers: money, time, relationships, health and peace of mind. Money covers saving money and earning it. Time covers reclaiming hours and creating open space in a diary. Relationships covers the people in a client's life, and whether a service brings people closer, helps them communicate, or helps them through a change. Health covers wellbeing, and it carries the most risk, because any health claim must be true and supported by reasonable grounds. The ACCC's advertising guide (July 2021) says health and therapeutic claims need reasonable grounds, usually scientific evidence. Do not promise treatment. Peace of mind covers reducing worry, knowing a job is done properly, and having someone to call when something goes wrong.

instruction.heading: Find the triggers your group responds to
instruction.body: Do not guess. Collect about ten real enquiries, reviews or messages from the group you serve, or from people very like them, and mark which trigger each message shows. Pay attention to the words clients use, because those words usually name the trigger. Count the marks, rank the triggers, and choose one or two to lead with. A trigger can matter without being the lead reason, so keep the others in your file for later messages.

instruction.heading: Write the message around the trigger, with honest proof
instruction.body: For each chosen trigger, write one message that names the client's situation, describes the service in plain words, gives one piece of proof you hold, and offers a clear next step. Keep urgency honest. Give a date only if it is real, and a price only if it is the price you charge. Avoid false deadlines and invented scarcity, because they damage trust and may breach consumer law. The ACCC guide says limited-time offers and short supply must be stated clearly and must be genuinely available.

instruction.heading: Money and health claims need the most care
instruction.body: A money claim, such as a saving, needs the numbers behind it. Price comparisons such as was/now or two-price claims need records behind them, according to the ACCC guide. A health claim needs more care still. A service can describe what a session includes and how it is run. As a working rule, do not claim to treat, cure or prevent any condition. Australian health-claim rules have not been checked against an official source in this lesson, so check with the relevant regulator before using any health wording. The service should point people with a health concern towards their own health provider. Follow-up email or text that promotes the service can fall under the Spam Act, which requires consent and an unsubscribe option (ACMA).

procedure: Write the target group in one line
Collect about ten real enquiries, reviews or messages from that group
Mark each message with the buying trigger it shows, and count the marks
Choose one or two triggers to lead with, based on the count
Write one message per chosen trigger, with the client's situation, a plain description, one proof item and one next step
Check each claim against evidence, and remove any money or health claim you cannot support
Record the trigger counts, the messages and the evidence references

workedExamples.situation: A dog walker in a Melbourne suburb notices that most enquiries come from commuters who mention long working days. The enquiries point to the time trigger and the peace-of-mind trigger.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which trigger should lead the next message, and what proof should it include?
workedExamples.reasoning: Time should lead, because commuters name it in their own words. Peace of mind comes second, supported by the handover record and a photo update that the walker has actually sent before. The walker describes the walk times and the update routine, and sends messages only to clients who have agreed to receive updates.

workedExamples.situation: A massage therapist wants to describe a relaxation session as a fix for back pain.
workedExamples.reasoning: A claim to fix back pain is a health and treatment claim. The lesson gives no evidence for it, and ACCC guidance says health claims need reasonable grounds. A safer message describes the relaxation session and what it includes, and invites clients with a back concern to see their own health provider first.

equipmentAndPpe: No PPE is needed for this lesson
A file of past enquiries and reviews, with names and contact details removed
A notebook for the trigger counts

commonErrors.error: Leading with a feature list and calling it a trigger
commonErrors.prevention: Start from the client's situation, name the trigger, then name the feature that answers it.

commonErrors.error: Using all five triggers in every message
commonErrors.prevention: Lead with one or two triggers that are supported by evidence you hold.

commonErrors.error: Writing health claims that no evidence supports
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the session, avoid treatment claims, and refer health concerns to the client's own provider.

commonErrors.error: Quoting a real client's words publicly without permission
commonErrors.prevention: Remove names and get the client's written consent before using their words publicly. Whether the Privacy Act applies depends on the business's turnover and activities; check the OAIC small business guidance.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not make treatment, cure or prevention claims. Health-claim wording for fitness and wellbeing services has not been checked against an official source (see sourceReferences).

Consumer law: misleading or pressure-based advertising, including false urgency and unverified price or saving claims, may breach the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC advertising guide (July 2021) covers limited-time offers and price-comparison claims; check its current version with the regulator before relying on it.
Spam Act: marketing messages sent by email or text need consent, accurate sender identification and a free unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days (ACMA).

qualityStandard: The trigger ranking is based on at least ten real enquiries or messages, with the counts recorded
Each message names one trigger, one proof item and one next step
No health claim is made without evidence, and no message uses false urgency
documentationEvidence: Trigger count sheet with the source messages, names removed
Message drafts for each lead trigger, with an evidence reference for each claim
Consent record for any client words or any follow-up contact
summary: A buying trigger is the reason a client acts, and the message should name it
The five common triggers are money, time, relationships, health and peace of mind
Rank triggers using real enquiries, and lead with one or two
Keep urgency and health claims honest, and check consent before any follow-up

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement describes a buying trigger?
options: The reason a client acts, which a message can speak to
The price a business charges for a standard session
The legal form a business uses when it registers

knowledgeChecks.question: A relaxation service is writing a message about health. Which approach is correct?
options: Promise to relieve a named medical condition and say it will work in a single session
Describe the session, and suggest that clients with a health concern speak to their own health provider
Quote a study figure with no source attached and say it proves the result for everyone

knowledgeChecks.question: How should the triggers to lead with be chosen?
options: Use all five triggers in every message and send each one by text
Lead with whichever sounds most urgent to the owner
Rank the triggers from real enquiries, and lead with one or two

officialReferences.title: ACMA: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool (WebFetch): marketing messages need consent from each recipient, express or inferred, and consent cannot be requested by electronic message; every commercial electronic message needs an unsubscribe option that is free, honoured within 5 working days, functional for at least 30 days and needs no account or login; sender identity and contact details must be accurate for at least 30 days.

officialReferences.title: ACCC: Advertising and selling guide, a guide for business
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool (WebFetch), first 100,000 of about 123,600 characters. It is a regulator's guide, not the text of the Australian Consumer Law. It covers: limited-time offers and short supply must be stated clearly and must be genuinely available (bait advertising and special offers); was/now and two-price claims must not mislead and need records; claims about the future need reasonable grounds; health and therapeutic claims need reasonable grounds, usually scientific evidence; premium claims must be substantiated.

officialReferences.title: ACCC: False or misleading claims (general guidance, not health-claim rules)
officialReferences.covers: ACCC general guidance on premium claims: therapeutic or health-related claims must be true, accurate and based on reasonable grounds, and the business must be able to prove them. The page does not address health-claim wording for fitness or other services specifically. Publisher: ACCC.
